summary: Defines the BGP Encapsulation SAFI and the Tunnel Encapsulation attribute. They let BGP speakers agree on how a packet should be encapsulated when it crosses to the next hop. It was later replaced by RFC 9012.

plainLanguage.summary: Sometimes a packet must be put in a special envelope for part of its trip. This note lets two routers agree on which envelope to use and how to open it. It was later replaced by RFC 9012.

what is the tunnel encapsulation attribute
subtitle: Let routers agree on how to wrap packets for tunneling.

tldr.problem: When a router needs to send a packet to a distant next hop through a tunnel (because intermediate routers do not have routes), it needs to know which tunneling protocol to use and how to fill in the tunnel header fields like session IDs or encryption keys. Manual configuration of this information for every next hop is cumbersome.
tldr.mechanism: BGP Encapsulation SAFI (Subsequent Address Family Identifier) lets a router advertise its encapsulation preferences using BGP updates. An attribute carries tunnel type, session IDs, encryption keys, and other protocol-specific parameters. A color extended community can indicate which tunnel to use for which traffic.
tldr.outcome: Routers can now automatically agree on encapsulation methods and parameters without manual configuration, enabling flexible tunnel-based networks.

today: RFC 5512 is a Proposed Standard that was obsoleted by RFC 9012, which provides an updated specification of BGP Encapsulation SAFI with improvements and clarifications.

sections.title: The Encapsulation Problem
sections.content:
BGP is used to exchange routes across the Internet. Normally, a router receives a route announcement that says "packets to prefix D are best reached through next hop R", and it forwards packets to R directly. However, in some scenarios the intermediate routers between the current router and R do not have a route to R itself, or do not support the address family of D. In these cases, the packet must be encapsulated (wrapped in a tunnel) and sent through the tunnel to R.

Different tunneling protocols exist for this purpose: GRE (Generic Routing Encapsulation), L2TPv3 (Layer Two Tunneling Protocol version 3), and IP in IP. Some of these protocols require session IDs, encryption keys, or other parameters to be set up. Manually configuring these parameters at every ingress router for every tunnel endpoint is impractical. RFC 5512 solves this by allowing the tunnel endpoint to advertise its encapsulation requirements via BGP itself.
sections.plainLanguage: A router might need to wrap a packet in a special header to send it far away. Asking every other router to set up that wrapping by hand is tedious. Instead, the receiving router can announce what kind of wrapping to use, and everyone learns it automatically.

sections.title: BGP Encapsulation SAFI
sections.content:
The specification introduces a new BGP SAFI (Subsequent Address Family Identifier) value 7 called the Encapsulation SAFI. When a router advertises an Encapsulation SAFI update, the NLRI (Network Layer Reachability Information) contains just the router's own address. The actual encapsulation information is carried in a new BGP attribute called the Tunnel Encapsulation Attribute (type code 23).

This design has a key advantage: because the encapsulation information is separate from the routes themselves, a change in encapsulation parameters requires only one BGP update instead of sending new updates for every prefix. Conversely, when a prefix changes, the encapsulation information need not be re-advertised. The attribute is an optional transitive attribute, so it passes through intermediate BGP speakers (like route reflectors) that do not understand it, enabling new encapsulation types to be added without reconfiguring intermediate systems.
sections.plainLanguage: A router announces its wrapping method separately from the routes it advertises. If the wrapping method changes, only one announcement needs to go out. If the routes change, the wrapping announcement does not need to be sent again.

sections.title: The Tunnel Encapsulation Attribute
sections.content:
The Tunnel Encapsulation Attribute contains one or more TLVs (Type-Length-Value encodings), each describing a tunnel technology. Each TLV holds a tunnel type (such as L2TPv3, GRE, or IP in IP) and a length field, followed by sub-TLVs describing protocol-specific details. The Encapsulation sub-TLV holds the session ID and optional cookie for L2TPv3, or the GRE key for GRE tunnels. The Protocol Type sub-TLV indicates which payload protocol (IPv4, IPv6, MPLS) will be sent through the tunnel.

For example, an egress router might advertise three L2TPv3 tunnels with different session IDs, one for IPv4 traffic, one for IPv6, and one for MPLS traffic. Ingress routers use this information to correctly format the tunnel header for each packet type. An optional Color sub-TLV allows the tunnel to be colored; the router can then attach a Color Extended Community to payload prefixes to indicate which tunnel to use for traffic to those prefixes.
sections.plainLanguage: The announcement says "use this protocol, with this session number, for this kind of traffic." Different tunnels can be advertised for different traffic types, and colors can label them so a router knows which one to pick.

sections.title: The Encapsulation Extended Community
sections.content:
For encapsulation protocols where no parameters need to be signaled (such as plain GRE without a key), a simpler mechanism is provided: the BGP Encapsulation Extended Community. This is an optional transitive extended community that can be attached to UPDATE messages carrying payload prefixes. It simply specifies a tunnel type to be used for those prefixes. The receiving router looks for a matching Encapsulation SAFI update from the same originator to get the actual encapsulation information.

This approach is useful when the tunnel mechanism does not require complex setup but the egress router still wants to signal to ingress routers which protocol to use. If both an Encapsulation Extended Community and colored tunnel TLVs are present, local policy at the ingress router determines which tunnel to select.
sections.plainLanguage: If the wrapping method is simple and does not need special numbers, a router can just say "use GRE" without extra details. Other routers look up the GRE setup information separately.

sections.title: Practical Use and Security
sections.content:
The specification is designed for softwire scenarios where encapsulation allows connectivity across address family boundaries or where parts of the network do not carry all route types. For instance, the core of a network might be IPv6-only while edge routers connect IPv4 hosts, requiring IPv4-in-IPv6 encapsulation. Multi-vendor deployments can use colors to classify tunnel types: routers supporting GRE are colored one way, those supporting L2TPv3 another way, allowing each ingress router to choose based on its capabilities and policy.

Security depends on the integrity of BGP updates. If an attacker can modify Encapsulation SAFI updates or color communities, packets can be misdirected, misdelivered, or dropped. The specification inherits security considerations from the underlying tunnel protocols and recommends treating BGP encapsulation information with the same care as any other BGP data.
sections.plainLanguage: Different routers might support different wrapping methods. Color labels let each router pick the method it understands. If someone changes the announcement, packets go to the wrong place, so these announcements should be protected like any other BGP data.

fields.name: Sub-TLV Length
fields.desc: Length of the value field in octets.

fields.name: Session ID
fields.desc: Non-zero 4-octet value assigned by the egress router.

fields.name: Cookie
fields.desc: Variable-length value (0-8 octets) for additional session validation.
